'''Eugenia María del Pino Veintimilla''' (born April 19, 1945, [[Quito]], [[Ecuador]]) is a [[developmental biology|developmental biologist]] at the [[Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador|Pontificia Universidad Catolica del Ecuador]] (Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador) in Quito.<ref name="biologia.puce.edu.ec">{{cite web |url=http://www.biologia.puce.edu.ec/azul.php?c=239 |title=Eugenia del Pino - Ciencias Biológicas PUCE |accessdate=2010-12-03 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719133919/http://www.biologia.puce.edu.ec/azul.php?c=239 |archivedate=2011-07-19 }}</ref> She was the first Ecuadorian citizen to be elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] (2006).<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/eugenia-m-del-pino-zkrzot/|title=Eugenia del Pino|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> 
She was awarded the 2019 Prize of the Latin American Society for Developmental Biology<ref name=":1" /> for her strong contributions to research in Ecuador, and in general to promoting Developmental Biology in Latin America.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://lasdb-development.org/pages/prize.html|title=LASDB - Latin American Society for Developmental Biology|website=lasdb-development.org|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Del Pino was born and grew up in Quito, Ecuador. She received a licentiate degree from the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador ([[Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador|PUCE]]), Quito 1967.<ref name="cncultura.gob.ec">{{cite web |url=http://www.cncultura.gob.ec/index.php?option=com_content&view=category&layout=blog&id=18&Itemid=153 |title=Ganadores (Biografías) |accessdate=2013-04-02 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20130412112426/http://www.cncultura.gob.ec/index.php?option=com_content&view=category&layout=blog&id=18&Itemid=153 |archivedate=2013-04-12 }}</ref> She then studied in the 
United States of America and holds a M.Sc. [[Vassar College]], 1969, and a Ph.D. [[Emory University]], 1972.
Upon completion of the doctorate she returned to Ecuador and joined the faculty the 
Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador in Quito.<ref name="cncultura.gob.ec"/>

She was professor of Biology from 1972 to 2013. She is a professor emerita at PUCE since 2013 and engages in the theme of her scientific career, the analysis of frog early development.

She served as Head of Biological Sciences, from 1973–1975.

With a fellowship from the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]] she did research at the [[German Cancer Research Center]], [[Heidelberg]], 1984–1985. She was [[Fulbright fellow|Fulbright Fellow]] at the laboratory of Prof. [[Joseph G. Gall|Joseph Gall]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://emb.carnegiescience.edu/science/faculty/joseph-gall|title=Joseph Gall|last=Science|first=Carnegie|website=Department of Embryology|access-date=2019-11-29}}</ref> [[Carnegie Institution of Washington|Carnegie Institution for Science, Department of Embryology in Baltimore, MD, USA]], 1990.<ref name="biologia.puce.edu.ec" />

Eugenia del Pino is recognized as the premier developmental biologist of Latin America by the Latin American Society for Developmental Biology.<ref name=":1" />

== Research and career ==

Hers is a story of relentless determination and embracing every opportunity that was offered to her by a number of institutions. She was trained to become a High School Teacher at PUCE, at the time when President John F. Kennedy started the [[Alliance for Progress]] Program with Latin America. Some equipment and a few professors were sent to Ecuador to help in the training of high school science teachers. One of her professors, Dr. Cándida Acosta, encouraged her to apply for a scholarship to do graduate studies in the United States of America. She received a scholarship from the Latin American Scholarship Program of American Universities (LASPAU)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.laspau.harvard.edu/es/|title=Laspau – Connecting Higher Education Across the Americas|website=www.laspau.harvard.edu|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref> and an international fellowship from the [[American Association of University Women]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aauw.org/|title=AAUW: Empowering Women Since 1881|website=AAUW: Empowering Women Since 1881|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref> for her graduate studies in the US. Eugenia obtained a [[Master of Science]] from [[Vassar College]] and went on to [[Emory University]] in [[Atlanta]] to obtain a Ph.D with a great mentor, Asa Alan Humphries, Jr. Her dissertation dealt with the role of the egg-jelly on the fertilization of ''Xenopus [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jez.1401850112 laevis]''. Upon returning to Ecuador in 1972 she became professor of Biology at [[Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador|PUCE]], her original University in Quito, and developed her scientific career in Ecuador.

Through her, [[Developmental biology|Developmental Biology]] blossomed in a most unlikely place: Not having any funds to buy ''[[African clawed frog|Xenopus laevis]]'', she came across a frog, called ''[[Andean marsupial tree frog|Gastrotheca riobambae]]'', in the very gardens of her University. A frog that she developed into a premier system to study the evolution of developmental adaptations. ''Gastrotheca'' is a [[marsupial]] frog that carries its eggs in a pouch on her back, where they are pushed in by the male with his hindlimbs. This terrestrial form of reproduction solely occurs in the Latin American frogs of the family Hemiphractidae.<ref name=pmid23429349>{{cite journal |last1=Schmid |first1=M. |last2=Steinlein |first2=C. |last3=Bogart |first3=J.P. |last4=Feichtinger |first4=W. |last5=Haaf |first5=T. |last6=Nanda |first6=I. |last7=Del Pino |first7=E.M. |last8=Duellman |first8=W.E. |last9=Hedges |first9=S.B. |s2cid=22421412 |title=The Hemiphractid Frogs. Phylogeny, Embryology, Life History, and Cytogenetics |journal=Cytogenetic and Genome Research |date=2012 |volume=138 |issue=2–4 |pages=69–83 |doi=10.1159/000343460 |pmid=23429349 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Out of the intense competition for reproductive sites in the South American rainforest had evolved over 90 species of these frogs, in which the female incubates her embryos inside her body bringing parallelism to mammalian reproduction.<ref name=pmid23429349/>

Marsupial frog embryos develop under saline conditions typically found in the body in contrast with the aquatic mode of development found in ''Xenopus'' and many other frogs.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Del Pino |first1=Eugenia |title=The early development of Gastrotheca riobambae and Colostethus machalilla, frogs with terrestrial reproductive modes |url=https://www.lifescitrc.org/resource.cfm?submissionID=3000 |website=LifeSciTRC.org |date=April 27, 2005 }}</ref> Traditional frogs and marsupial frogs also differ in how their embryos excrete waste. Free-swimming tadpoles excrete ammonia, which would be toxic if accumulated in close quarters. Eugenia del Pino discovered that marsupial frog embryos excrete urea instead of ammonia.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alcocer |first1=Iliana |last2=Santacruz |first2=Ximena |last3=Steinbeisser |first3=Herbert |last4=Thierauch |first4=Karl-Heinz |last5=Del Pino |first5=Eugenia M. |title=Ureotelism as the prevailing mode of nitrogen excretion in larvae of the marsupial frog Gastrotheca riobambae (Fowler) (Anura, Hylidae) |journal=Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part A: Physiology |date=January 1992 |volume=101 |issue=2 |pages=229–231 |doi=10.1016/0300-9629(92)90527-w |pmid=1348458 }}</ref> She discovered that addition of urea, which reaches high levels in the pouch, allows eggs to develop outside of the marsupial frog mother.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Del Pino |first1=Eugenia M. |last2=Alcocer |first2=Iliana |last3=Grunz |first3=Horst |title=Urea is Necessary for the Culture of Embryos of the Marsupial Frog Gastrotheca riobambae, and is Tolerated by Embryos of the Aquatic Frog Xenopus laevis. (ureotelism/urea concentration in frog blood/culture of frog embryos/mesoderm induction) |journal=Development, Growth and Differentiation |date=February 1994 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=73–80 |doi=10.1111/j.1440-169X.1994.00073.x |doi-access=free |pmid=37282245 }}</ref> Urea is a nitrogenous waste product that marsupial frog embryos use for water retention under the water stress conditions of the maternal pouch.

Eggs of these frogs are very large, ranging from 3 to 10&nbsp;mm in diameter in different species, and contain the nutrients needed for development up to metamorphosis.<ref name=pmid29305906>{{cite journal |last1=Del Pino |first1=Eugenia M. |s2cid=300036 |title=The extraordinary biology and development of marsupial frogs (Hemiphractidae) in comparison with fish, mammals, birds, amphibians and other animals |journal=Mechanisms of Development |date=December 2018 |volume=154 |pages=2–11 |doi=10.1016/j.mod.2017.12.002 |pmid=29305906 |doi-access=free }}</ref> She found that ''Gastrotheca'' develops much like a chick embryo on the surface of the yolk. However, instead of a primitive streak there is a circular blastopore surrounded by an embryonic disc.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Del Pino |first1=Eugenia M. |last2=Elinson |first2=Richard P. |s2cid=4360114 |title=A novel development pattern for frogs: gastrulation produces an embryonic disk |journal=Nature |date=December 1983 |volume=306 |issue=5943 |pages=589–591 |doi=10.1038/306589a0 |bibcode=1983Natur.306..589D }}</ref> Surprisingly, extension starts only after involution at the [[Gastrulation|blastopore]] is concluded, demonstrating that these important movements can be dissociated from gastrulation itself.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Del Pino |first1=Eugenia M. |title=The Expression of Brachyury (T) during Gastrulation in the Marsupial FrogGastrotheca riobambae |journal=Developmental Biology |date=July 1996 |volume=177 |issue=1 |pages=64–72 |doi=10.1006/dbio.1996.0145 |pmid=8660877 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  Her analyses revealed extensive modularity in the developmental processes that guide the blastopore closure and [[notochord]] elongation in amphibians, features that correlate with reproductive modes and ecological adaptations.<ref name=pmid29305906/>

The flat embryos of ''Gastrotheca'' extend cranial [[neural crest]] cell-streams<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Del Pino |first1=EM |last2=Medina |first2=A |title=Neural development in the marsupial frog Gastrotheca riobambae. |journal=The International Journal of Developmental Biology |date=July 1998 |volume=42 |issue=5 |pages=723–31 |pmid=9712527 }}</ref> and branchial arches. Part of the neural crest becomes the "bell gills" that form a rich network of capillaries that surround the embryo in the pouch and exchange gases with the maternal circulation, while still separated by the egg envelope.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=DELPINO |first1=EUGENIA M. |last2=GALARZA |first2=MARÍA L. |last3=DE ALBUJA |first3=CARMEN M. |last4=HUMPHRIES |first4=A. A. |title=The Maternal Pouch and Development in the Marsupial Frog Gastrotheca Riobambae (Fowler) |journal=The Biological Bulletin |date=December 1975 |volume=149 |issue=3 |pages=480–491 |doi=10.2307/1540381 |jstor=1540381 |pmid=29324196 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/4355 }}</ref> This is a kind of amphibian version of a placenta without a uterus.

Eugenia del Pino studied many other marsupial frogs and found a Venezuelan one called ''[[Flectonotus pygmaeus]]'' that has adapted to its large egg by having [[oocyte]]s that at early stages have up to 3000 meiotic nuclei in a single cell. The many nuclei are gradually lost until in the mature yolky oocyte only a single one remains, forming a single germinal [https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.2307/1541122 vesicle]. Eugenia's discovery of the amazing biological adaptations of marsupial frogs lead to a famous [[Scientific American]] Article in 1989.<ref name="Pino, E. M 1989">Del Pino, E. M. Marsupial Frogs. Scientific American Volume 260. Number 5. Pages: 110-118 (May 1989)</ref>

Her work brought her election to the Latin American Academy of Sciences,<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.idealist.org/es/ong/ded1bdd2a11b42908d7b19725e8ccf24-academia-de-ciencias-de-america-latina-acal-caracas|title=Academia de Ciencias de América Latina · ACAL|website=www.idealist.org|language=es|access-date=2019-11-27}}</ref> [[The World Academy of Sciences]] for the Advancement of Science in Developing Countries,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://twas.org/|title=TWAS|website=TWAS|language=en|access-date=2019-11-27}}</ref> and in 2006 she became the first member of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA<ref name=":0" /> from Ecuador. She received the [[L'Oreal-UNESCO Award for Women in Science|L’Oreal-Unesco Prize for Women in Science for Latin America]]. Eugenia's life shows us how identifying an interesting biological problem and unraveling its mechanism can bring science to any country that allows for creativity.

Eugenia del Pino established an entire school of Biology in Ecuador focused in evolutionary developmental adaptations.<ref>{{Citation|last=Del Pino|first=Eugenia M.|chapter=Embryogenesis of Marsupial Frogs (Hemiphractidae), and the Changes that Accompany Terrestrial Development in Frogs|date=2019|pages=379–418|editor-last=Tworzydlo|editor-first=Waclaw|series=Results and Problems in Cell Differentiation|publisher=Springer International Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-030-23459-1_16|pmid=31598865|isbn=978-3-030-23459-1|editor2-last=Bilinski|editor2-first=Szczepan M.|title=Evo-Devo: Non-model Species in Cell and Developmental Biology|volume=68|s2cid=204032186 }}</ref>

== Teaching and contributions to society ==
Eugenia del Pino introduced the field of Developmental Biology to Ecuador and for a long time the PUCE, her home institution, was the only University in Ecuador with a theoretical and practical undergraduate course in this subject,<ref name=pmid12705669>{{cite journal |last1=Del Pino |first1=Eugenia M |title=Developmental biology in Ecuador: a 30-year teaching experience. |journal=The International Journal of Developmental Biology |date=2003 |volume=47 |issue=2–3 |pages=189–92 |pmid=12705669 |url=http://www.intjdevbiol.com/paper.php?doi=12705669 }}</ref> and her laboratory was the only highly productive Developmental Biology research laboratory.<ref name=pmid12705669/> Her research programs were mainly driven by undergraduate students, as no graduate programs were available in Ecuador at the time.

Scientific collaboration was one of her strengths. She partnered with scientists from USA, Japan, UK and Germany. She did so informally, or through programs including the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]] and [[Fulbright fellowships]]. Her productive scientific career resulted in the training of what is now an active generation of Latin American scientists. Her success results from her dedication and ability to train undergraduates in research. Her publication record is a testimony to her scientific commitment to undergraduate training, as many co-authors were her own undergraduate students.<ref name=pmid12705669/> Eugenia del Pino trained over 300 students through both her teaching and research.

Ecuador was one of the few countries in Latin America that did not have an Academy of Sciences. For this reason, Eugenia invited several colleagues to discuss the possibility of establishing the National Academy of Sciences of Ecuador (a.k.a. ACE because of its Spanish acronym).{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}} She and her colleagues drafted the statutes and obtained the legal recognition from the Government of Ecuador. In 2013, the Secretariat of Science and Technology of Ecuador recognized the ACE.<ref>https://www.educacionsuperior.gob.ec/ SENESCYT</ref> The six colleagues became the Founding Members of ACE. She served as Vice President of ACE from 2013 to 2016. The ACE membership grew in the following years, and has more than 50 Fellows. ACE provides recognition to its fellows, allows communication between Ecuadorian scientists, and seeks exchanges with institutions at home and abroad.{{Citation needed|date=May 2023}}

For about 25 years del Pino contributed to education for conservation of the [[Galápagos Islands|Galápagos Archipelago]]. She helped the Charles Darwin Foundation for the Galápagos Islands<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=https://www.darwinfoundation.org/en/|title=Charles Darwin Foundation|website=www.darwinfoundation.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2019-11-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181130004344/https://www.darwinfoundation.org/en/|archive-date=2018-11-30|url-status=dead}}</ref> in the establishment of a program of scholarships for Ecuadorian students in the Galápagos Islands.<ref>Annual Report 2009 of the Charles Darwin Foundation. Special issue, page 10. Available at {{cite web|url=http://www.darwinfoundation.org/english/_upload/annual_report_2009.pdf|title=Annual Report 2009|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20101119104606/http://darwinfoundation.org/english/_upload/annual_report_2009.pdf|archivedate=2010-11-19|accessdate=2010-12-05}}.</ref> She served as Vice President of the Charles Darwin Foundation for several years in the 1990s. Later, due to time limitations she withdrew from the Galápagos conservation activities.

Her work has made her a figure of importance in the Science of Ecuador<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=https://ccq.ec/|title=Cámara de Comercio de Quito – La cámara contigo|language=es|access-date=2019-11-27}}</ref> and Latin America.<ref name=":1" />
